phase1.intro:
So far every error you've caught has been one Java already knew about. But what happens when the thing going wrong is specific to YOUR blueprint?

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: How do I actually build my own exception?
dialogue: [[key:That's exactly what a custom exception is for]] — "Insufficient funds" isn't a Java concept, it's a banking concept, so we build InsufficientFundsException specifically for it.

Building one is simpler than it looks: you extend either [[term:Exception]] or [[term:RuntimeException]], and call `super(message)` in your constructor so the built-in error machinery still works underneath. That's really it.

stickyNote.flavor: 🏗️ invent the error, in your own words
stickyNote.definition: A custom exception extends Exception or RuntimeException and calls super(message) in its constructor — everything else is optional.

topics.buttonText: Should mine extend Exception or RuntimeException?
dialogue: [[term:Checked]] (extends Exception) is for things that can genuinely happen even when the code is correct — a file might not exist, an account might legitimately run low on funds. Java insists: "you don't get to pretend this can't happen."

[[term:Unchecked]] (extends RuntimeException) is for programmer mistakes — passing -100 as an amount is a bug, not something that "just happens." [[warn:Mixing these up is a genuinely common mistake]].

stickyNote.flavor: 🎯 legitimate real-world case vs. programmer bug
stickyNote.definition: extends Exception for things that can happen even with correct code (checked). extends RuntimeException for programmer mistakes (unchecked).

topics.buttonText: Does the name of my exception actually matter?
dialogue: One habit worth building now: name your exception after what actually went wrong — InsufficientFundsException, not Error1 or BankException. Whoever catches it later will thank you, and that whoever is often future-you.

stickyNote.flavor: 📝 name it after what actually went wrong
stickyNote.definition: Name custom exceptions specifically (InsufficientFundsException), not generically (Error1) — future readers will thank you.

phase1.openingDialogue: When Java has no name for what went wrong in your program, you build your own exception — checked for real-world cases, unchecked for bugs. 🏗️

phase2.errorMessage:
MyException.java:9: error: cannot find symbol
    void validate(int value) throws MyException {  // ERROR!
                                    ^
  symbol:   class MyException
  location: class Validator
MyException.java:11: error: incompatible types: MyException cannot be converted to Throwable
            throw new MyException("Invalid value");
            ^
2 errors
phase2.explanation:
MyException never actually extends Exception or RuntimeException — it's just a plain class that happens to have the word "Exception" in its name. [[warn:Java doesn't care what you NAME a class]] — it only cares what it actually extends.

That's why both throws MyException and catch (MyException e) fail to compile: as far as Java is concerned, MyException isn't a Throwable at all, so it's not legal to throw or catch it — same as trying to throw a String or an int.

[[key:Custom exceptions MUST extend Exception or RuntimeException]] (or one of their subclasses) — there's no way around this part, it's what makes Java's throw/catch machinery recognize your class as an exception at all.
phase2.openingDialogue: Watch what happens when an "exception" forgets to actually BE one~

phase3.openingDialogue: Let's give a shop its own error vocabulary, together.

mcq.question:
Which pair correctly matches the exception type to when you'd use it?

A) Checked (extends Exception) for programmer bugs; Unchecked (extends RuntimeException) for things that can legitimately happen
B) Checked (extends Exception) for things that can legitimately happen; Unchecked (extends RuntimeException) for programmer bugs
C) It doesn't matter which one you extend, as long as the name ends in "Exception"
D) Custom exceptions don't need to extend anything, Java infers it from the name

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a custom exception class AgeException (extends Exception).

Create a Person class with:
• Fields: name, age
• Constructor validates:
  - If age < 0 or age > 150 → throw AgeException
• Method: vote() — can only vote if age >= 18 → throw AgeException if not

In main, test with valid and invalid ages.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: Java's checked-exception rule is actually a famous point of disagreement among language designers — most other major languages (Python, JavaScript, C#, even Kotlin, which otherwise runs on the same JVM as Java) skipped checked exceptions entirely. Some engineers love that Java forces you to acknowledge what can go wrong; others find it forces a lot of boilerplate try/catch for errors nobody has a good way to handle anyway. Now that you've built one of each kind yourself, you get to have an informed opinion about which side you're on.
phase5.openingDialogue: Before you go — a little language-design drama~

hoverNotes.InsufficientFundsException: A checked exception (extends Exception) — something that can legitimately happen even in correct code, so Java forces callers to handle or declare it.
hoverNotes.NegativeAmountException: An unchecked exception (extends RuntimeException) — signals a programmer mistake, so Java doesn't force every caller to catch it.
